projects.title: DIY MP3 Player
projects.summary: A simplified MP3 player constructed from an Arduino Nano and a passive (piezo disk) buzzer soldered on a perfboard. The goal was to hardcode the melodic information from a couple of songs to the nano, with said melodies then being played through the buzzer. Since this was a gift to someone, I also created some custom bitmaps for the OLED display.
projects.description:
This project was a Valentine's gift for a certain someone, and I have to admit that this was just about the most work I have ever put into a present period. I’d say that, given my inexperience, the soldering was the hardest part (particularly at 2:30 am when I realized I had unwittingly soldered the same 2 sides of all of the buttons together).

At first, I was overly preoccupied with the harsh sound the buzzer produced, since the Nano outputs a square wave (on the PWM pins) on the order of 0 to 5v that contains some understandably sharp edges. I chalked this up to the square waves generating harmonics, whereas a more palatable sine wave has just one frequency.

I believe most of these passive buzzers resonate around 2–4 kHz, so I thought it would be prudent to make a LPF that would clip the higher end of the range, resulting in a more decent sounding output. Over the course of a couple of days, I had to forage for some specific capacitor values in our EE lab. Their stores were apparently raided by like-minded individuals; I settled for wiring up 4 100nF caps in parallel, since it produced the best sounding result from what little supplies I could salvage. Turns out that after soldering, the buzzer, for whatever reason, ended up sounding fine without the LPF anyway.

Another tricky part was the software and finding a way to extract the relevant frequency, duration, and timing information from the songs. I picked 3 different songs (Space Oddity by David Bowie, Mandy by Barry Manilow, and The Gambler by Kenny Rogers). I thought the easiest way to extract the relevant information would be by tampering with their MIDI files.

So after troubleshooting for whoever knows how long, I figured out that MIDI files have specific tracks that correspond to different elements of the score (e.g., Bass, Guitar, Melody, Chorus). These tracks aren’t universal insofar as track 5 always contains the “guitar” information for a different MIDI file, so you have to suss out which one is which. It turns out that the track called ‘vocals’ sounds most like the song (go figure).

One of the major complications with the buzzer was that at any given time, I would only be able to play 1 note at a time with the buzzer, so I needed to identify a single track on the MIDI. Knowing this, I created a script that obtained the relevant information from the specified track of the MIDI file. Then, instead of playing those notes on the buzzer immediately (and transferring the songs' data arrays from Python to C++ again and again), I made a script that played the notes in some .WAV format in the VSCode IDE. Since the vocal track contained pauses where there was no one singing, I then concatenated all the vocals, formatted it into C++, and then shipped them to the Arduino.

To obtain the custom OLED images on the screen, there was a tutorial on YouTube that I followed. A guy made a site that allowed you to upload an image and it would output a bitmap you could copy and paste.
